questions.prompt: P(r) = 5000(1 + r)¹⁰ with r > 0 is the value of an investment. Which reasoning shows, without calculating, that P(r) > 5000?
questions.prompt_markup: P(r) = 5000(1 + r)¹⁰ with r > 0 is the value of an investment. Which reasoning shows, without calculating, that P(r) > 5000?

choices.text: (1 + r)¹⁰ = 1 + r¹⁰ by distributing the exponent, and 1 + r¹⁰ is greater than 1 for r > 0, so P(r) > 5000.
1 + r > 1, so (1 + r)¹⁰ is a product of ten numbers greater than 1 and is greater than 1; 5000 times a number greater than 1 is greater than 5000.
The exponent 10 is greater than 1, so any positive number raised to the 10th power is greater than 1, and P(r) > 5000.

questions.correct_answer: 1 + r > 1, so (1 + r)¹⁰ is a product of ten numbers greater than 1 and is greater than 1; 5000 times a number greater than 1 is greater than 5000.
questions.grading_note: Treat (1 + r)¹⁰ as one quantity greater than 1. The others distribute a power over a sum, check one value, or use a false rule (0.5¹⁰ < 1).

questions.prompt: C(x) = 10 + 40/(x + 1) is a cost in dollars for x ≥ 0. Which reasoning shows that C(x) is always more than 10 and never more than 50?
questions.prompt_markup: C(x) = 10 + 40/(x + 1) is a cost in dollars for x ≥ 0. Which reasoning shows that C(x) is always more than 10 and never more than 50?

choices.text: 40/(x + 1) is at least 40 because x + 1 ≥ 1, so C(x) is at least 10 + 40 = 50 for every x ≥ 0.
40/(x + 1) can be 0, so C(x) can equal 10; it is at most 50 because 10 + 40 = 50.
C(0) = 50 and C(100) ≈ 10.4, and both are between 10 and 50, so every value of C(x) is between 10 and 50.
x + 1 ≥ 1, so 40/(x + 1) is positive and at most 40; adding 10 gives more than 10 and at most 50 (equal to 50 at x = 0).

questions.correct_answer: x + 1 ≥ 1, so 40/(x + 1) is positive and at most 40; adding 10 gives more than 10 and at most 50 (equal to 50 at x = 0).
questions.grading_note: Treat 40/(x + 1) as one positive quantity at most 40. The others check two values, reverse the inequality, or claim the fraction can be 0.

questions.prompt: The temperature of a drink is T(t) = 70 - 30(0.8)ᵗ °F after t minutes (t ≥ 0). Which reasoning explains why T(t) is always below 70 and gets closer to 70 as t grows?
questions.prompt_markup: The temperature of a drink is T(t) = 70 - 30(0.8)ᵗ °F after t minutes (t ≥ 0). Which reasoning explains why T(t) is always below 70 and gets closer to 70 as t grows?

choices.text: 30(0.8)ᵗ is always positive, so T < 70; (0.8)ᵗ shrinks toward 0 as t grows, so T approaches 70.
(0.8)ᵗ grows as t grows, so the amount 30(0.8)ᵗ grows, and T rises toward 70 from below without reaching it.
30(0.8)ᵗ becomes exactly 0 after enough minutes, and from then on T equals 70 and stops changing.
T(0) = 40 and T(10) ≈ 66.8 are both below 70 and rising, so T stays below 70 and approaches it.

questions.correct_answer: 30(0.8)ᵗ is always positive, so T < 70; (0.8)ᵗ shrinks toward 0 as t grows, so T approaches 70.
questions.grading_note: Treat 30(0.8)ᵗ as one positive, shrinking quantity. The others claim the power grows, claim it reaches 0, or reason from two values.

questions.prompt: f(x) = 3/(x² + 1). Which gives the greatest value of f(x) with a correct reason?
questions.prompt_markup: f(x) = 3/(x² + 1). Which gives the greatest value of f(x) with a correct reason?

choices.text: 4, at x = 1, because x² + 1 is smallest when x = 1.
3, at x = 0: x² + 1 ≥ 1, so 3/(x² + 1) ≤ 3, with equality only when x = 0.
3, at x = 0, because f(1) = 1.5 and f(2) = 0.6 are smaller.
There is no greatest value, because x² + 1 can be as large as we like.

questions.correct_answer: 3, at x = 0: x² + 1 ≥ 1, so 3/(x² + 1) ≤ 3, with equality only when x = 0.
questions.grading_note: The smallest denominator gives the largest value. The others check a few inputs only, confuse a large denominator with a large value, or misplace the smallest denominator.

sections.skill: Use single-entity reasoning to find horizontal asymptotes

branch.new_demand: Use the behavior of one part for large inputs to find and justify horizontal asymptotes of rational functions.
branch.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: the bounds found there become end behavior (asymptotes) of the graph.

questions.skill: Use single-entity reasoning to find horizontal asymptotes
questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: Why does y = 10 + 40/(x + 1) have the horizontal asymptote y = 10?
questions.prompt_markup: Why does y = 10 + 40/(x + 1) have the horizontal asymptote y = 10?

choices.text: The constant term of any rational expression, here 10, is always its horizontal asymptote.
As x grows without bound, 40/(x + 1) gets closer and closer to 0, so y gets closer to 10.
When x = -1 the fraction is undefined, so y = 10 there.
At x = 0, y = 10 + 40 = 50, and 50 is the asymptote shifted up by the 40 in the numerator.

questions.correct_answer: As x grows without bound, 40/(x + 1) gets closer and closer to 0, so y gets closer to 10.
questions.grading_note: The quotient 40/(x + 1) tends to 0. The others use a single point, a false rule (y = 10 + 40x/(x + 1) has asymptote 50), or confuse the vertical asymptote x = -1 with a value of y.
